brief.title: Reading the harbour wall
brief.audience: Museum trustees and the conservation committee
brief.objective: Fund a further season on the harbour wall before the sea takes context 114
brief.visualDirection: Authored for this deck; see creativeDirection.
brief.sourcePrompt: Showcase brief: Reading the harbour wall

narrative: By the end the trustees should fund one more season, because the sequence is legible now and will not be in two winters.

alternatives.name: Trench section
alternatives.thesis: The deck reads downward like a section drawing: newest at the top, evidence beneath
alternatives.differentiator: Uneven horizontal bands descending across the sequence; nothing is boxed and nothing is centred

alternatives.name: Finds tray
alternatives.thesis: Each slide is a tray of objects photographed from above
alternatives.differentiator: Scattered small objects on a large empty field
alternatives.rejectedBecause: A tray flattens the stratigraphy, and the stratigraphy is the argument

claims.claim: Context 114 cuts context 112, placing the rebuild after the harbour was already in use
The cliff edge has moved 2.9 m closer to the trench since 2019
At the current rate the eastern half of the trench is lost within two winters
claims.calculation: Remaining distance ÷ mean annual loss, rounded down

creativeDirection.name: Trench section
creativeDirection.concept: The deck reads downward the way a trench does: newest at the top, evidence beneath it
creativeDirection.rationale: The committee is being asked to trust a sequence, so the sequence should be the composition rather than a claim about one
creativeDirection.geometryLanguage: Torn horizontal bands of unequal depth. Nothing is boxed; the right edge stays ragged
creativeDirection.spatialRhythm: Each slide sits lower on the page than the one before it, until the last one stops
creativeDirection.materialLanguage: Paper stock, ink bleed, and the grain of a section drawing

strata.usage: One band per claim; never equal heights
avoid: Bands with square corners on all four sides

cut.description: A later feature slicing an earlier one
cut.meaning: Somebody changed their mind about the harbour

hard: No slide may centre its type
Every context number appears in the source archive
soft: Prefer one long sentence to three short ones

title: Reading the harbour wall
designIntent: Put the reader at the wall. The plate is full height; the type is a narrow column beside it, low.
composition: A tall section plate occupying the right two-fifths; one narrow column of type at the lower left.

alt: A vertical section through the harbour wall showing six bands of deposit from topsoil to bedrock

provenance.source: Abstract stratigraphic field generated for this showcase; not a photograph of a real site

text: Three seasons in, the sequence finally reads. The sea has two winters' worth of it left.

notes: Do not explain the plate. Let them look at it while you say the standfirst.

title: The sequence, read downward
designIntent: The one slide that is entirely the motif. Six bands of unequal depth, newest at the top.
composition: Six horizontal bands filling the page top to bottom, each labelled in its own left edge.

text: Depth is drawn to scale. 114 is thin and it is the whole argument: somebody cut into a wall that was already standing.

notes: Give them six seconds before you speak. The bands do the work.

title: Context 114 cuts context 112
designIntent: One block of type, low and left, in a page that is otherwise empty. The claim carries itself.
composition: A single paragraph at the lower left; a thin cut-line crossing the upper page.

text: The rebuild is later than the wall it repairs, which means the harbour was already in use when somebody decided it was the wrong shape. Every date in the archive moves with that one relationship.
Recorded in section, season two. Photographed and drawn; both are in the archive.

notes: This is the slide the committee will remember. Do not add anything to it.

title: What the sea has taken since 2019
designIntent: Short line of type, then the measurement. The chart is wide and low so it reads as a shoreline.
composition: One line of type high-left; a wide line chart occupying the lower half.

text: What the sea has taken since 2019
Two point nine metres of cliff edge, measured from the same three fixed stations every November.

alt: The cliff edge has moved from 9.4 m to 6.5 m from the trench edge between 2019 and 2025

text: Coastal monitoring survey, annual, measured each November from fixed stations.

notes: The line is nearly straight. Say so — it is why the forecast is credible.

title: What one more season buys
designIntent: The practical slide. A table in the middle band, nothing above it but a label.
composition: A table filling the middle of the page; a short note beneath it.

rows: Excavate and record the eastern half of the trench
Lift and conserve the dressed footing stones

text: The first row is the one the sea decides. The other three can be done in any year.

notes: Costs are the 2026 rates in the site archive appendix.

title: Two winters
designIntent: One sentence at display size in the middle of an empty page. The deck stops rather than concludes.
composition: A single band of type across the middle; a small qualifier at the foot.

text: Fund one more season, and the eastern half is recorded before it goes.
Two winters is a forecast, not a measurement. It assumes the mean annual loss holds; a single storm can take it sooner.
Decision requested at the June meeting.

notes: Say the qualifier out loud. The forecast is the weakest claim in the deck and they should hear that from you.
